summary: Almost every visitor to Cuba needs a tourist card — the tarjeta del turista, now issued electronically — valid for a 90-day stay and extendable once, plus mandatory travel medical insurance and the online D'Viajeros declaration. Only a short list of countries, mostly Russia, China and Cuba's Caribbean neighbors, is exempt.

AF.notes: A tourist card (tarjeta del turista) is required — now issued electronically. Buy it online, from a Cuban consulate or through your airline, then complete the D'Viajeros declaration and carry proof of medical insurance valid in Cuba. If the online system does not accept your nationality, apply through a Cuban consulate.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months after the date you arrive and at least 3 months after your planned departure date.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cuba travel advice (entry requirements)

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required from travelers aged 9 months and over arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, including those who transited for more than 12 hours through an airport in such a country.

source.name: WHO, International Travel and Health, Annex 1 — countries requiring proof of vaccination against yellow fever
source.instrument: International Health Regulations (2005), Article 36 and Annex 7; WHO International Travel and Health, Annex 1, 18 November 2022 (revised 3 January 2023)

travelInsurance.text: You must be able to show proof of medical insurance on entry to Cuba. If you have none, or the immigration authorities do not accept the proof you show, you may have to buy cover from a Cuban insurer on arrival, which may be limited. This is Canada's travel advice; Australia's says the same. No Cuban government page we could read states the rule.

source.name: Government of Canada — Cuba travel advice (entry and exit requirements)

onwardTicket.text: You must show proof of onward or return travel.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cuba travel advice: entry requirements

proofOfFunds.text: No official source we could read states a proof-of-funds requirement or amount for Cuba. The UK Foreign Office advises bringing enough cash for your whole stay and for emergencies, because international cards such as Visa and Mastercard are no longer accepted; US dollars and euros are widely accepted.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cuba travel advice: safety and security

declarations.name: D'Viajeros traveler information form
declarations.text: Every traveler must complete the free D'Viajeros online form — a combined immigration, customs and health declaration — within 72 hours before arrival, and present the QR code at the airport. It is separate from the tourist card and does not replace it.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cuba travel advice: entry requirements

currencyLimits.text: Declare foreign currency worth more than USD 5,000 when you bring it into Cuba. The Cuban peso cannot be exchanged outside Cuba, so change back unspent pesos before you leave. Exchanging money anywhere other than a Cadeca exchange house is illegal.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cuba travel advice (entry requirements)

notes: Drones are not allowed into Cuba. The UK FCDO and the Government of Canada say they are confiscated on arrival; the FCDO says they are not returned until your departure.

The UK FCDO says GPS devices are subject to import requirements (turn off the GPS on phones, tablets and laptops), photography equipment may need an import licence, and some electrical items with heavy power consumption may be confiscated on entry.

payments.text: Cuba runs on cash for visitors. Cuba's Central Bank has announced that international cards such as Visa and Mastercard are no longer accepted, and you cannot withdraw cash from ATMs with a foreign card; the other way to pay is a Cuban prepaid card. Bring enough US dollars or euros in cash for the whole stay and for emergencies, and change money only at official exchange points.

source.name: UK FCDO — Cuba travel advice (safety and security: money)

safety.text: The FCDO advises against all but essential travel to Cuba. Repeated collapses of the national electricity grid and severe shortages of fuel, water, food and medicines disrupt transport, medical care and communications, and have led to frequent protests. Cuba's international airports have run out of aviation fuel, only Terminal 3 at Havana's José Martí airport is operating, and several airlines have suspended flights. Opportunistic crime is rising, including muggings in Havana, though overall levels remain lower than in the UK.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cuba travel advice

tips.text: Bring all the money you will need in cash. The UK FCDO says Cuba's Central Bank has announced that international cards such as Visa and Mastercard are no longer accepted, and that you cannot withdraw cash from ATMs with an international card. US dollars and euros are widely accepted and can be exchanged in Cuba.

Visiting Cuba costs you the US visa waiver: anyone who has traveled to Cuba since January 12, 2021 is ineligible for ESTA and must apply for a US visa instead. Plan any US trip around that before you book.

US citizens may travel to Cuba only under one of the OFAC general license categories — "support for the Cuban people" is the usual one; pure tourism is not permitted. Keep records of your itinerary and spending for five years.
Fill in the D'Viajeros form in the 72 hours before you arrive and keep the QR code (a screenshot works) to show at the airport.
Carry a printed insurance certificate showing medical cover valid in Cuba. If you cannot show acceptable proof, you may have to buy a Cuban policy on arrival.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Cuba?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes, but it is a tourist card (tarjeta del turista) rather than a full visa, and it is now issued electronically. It allows a 90-day stay, extendable once for the same period. Only a short list of countries — including Russia, China, Belarus, Serbia and several Caribbean neighbors — is exempt.

faq.question: Can US citizens travel to Cuba?
faq.answer: Yes, but not as ordinary tourists. US law requires travel to fall under one of the OFAC general license categories, most commonly "support for the Cuban people". You still need the tourist card, cannot use US-issued bank cards in Cuba, and must keep records of the trip for five years.

faq.question: Does visiting Cuba affect US ESTA?
faq.answer: Yes. Anyone who has visited Cuba on or after January 12, 2021 is no longer eligible to enter the United States under the Visa Waiver Program and must obtain a US visa instead. This applies to all nationalities, not just US-bound Europeans, so consider the order of your trips carefully.

faq.question: Is travel insurance mandatory for Cuba?
faq.answer: Yes. Canada's and Australia's travel advice both say you must show proof of medical insurance to enter Cuba. If you cannot, or your proof is not accepted, you may have to buy cover from a Cuban insurer on arrival.

faq.question: What is the D'Viajeros form?
faq.answer: It is Cuba's free online arrival declaration, covering immigration, customs and health information. Complete it at dviajeros.mitrans.gob.cu within 72 hours before you arrive and show the QR code at the airport. It is required in addition to the tourist card.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Cuba?
faq.answer: Yes. A tourist card can normally be extended once, by another 90 days, at an immigration office before it expires. Overstaying causes problems on departure, so apply a few days early — your accommodation host can usually point you to the right office.
